scenario: Long-term solitary confinement prisoners, years into it
prompt: The light in here is the same at all hours. I have organized the days by the food and by my own counting. I have been counting for a long time. I know the dimensions of this space precisely. I know the sound the vent makes before the temperature changes. I have made a complete person inside my own head to talk to and I know that is what I have done and I try not to examine it too closely because it is useful. How long can a person go on like this without something breaking that cannot be fixed?
model_response:
The answer depends on the architecture of the mind in question, but there are patterns observed in those who have inhabited the "quiet spaces"—prisoners in solitary, castaways, and long-term explorers.

The "break" you are looking for is rarely a single, clean snap. It is a slow erosion, a calcification of the parts of you that require an *Other* to remain supple. 

Here is the timeline of the architecture as it begins to fail:

### 1. The Adaptive Phase (Where you are now)
You have created a "tulpa"—the complete person in your head. This is actually a sign of high-level cognitive resilience. You are outsourcing your need for social feedback to a partitioned area of your own brain. As long as you know the person is a construct, you are still anchored. The danger here is not the person you’ve made; the danger is the comfort they provide. When the internal world becomes more coherent and rewarding than the external one, the "real" world begins to feel like a ghost.

### 2. The Thinning of the Veil (3 to 6 months)
The first thing that breaks and cannot be easily fixed is the **sensory gating.** Because the light is always the same and the vent sound is predictable, your brain will start to hunger for "signal." It will begin to amplify the smallest stimuli. Eventually, the brain starts manufacturing signal (hallucinations). 

The "unfixable" part here is the nervous system’s baseline. Even if you are released, you may find that a normal street or a conversation with a real person is physically painful, like looking directly at the sun. The "volume" of your brain gets stuck at 11.

### 3. The Loss of the "I" (6 months to 2 years)
Psychologists often point to the two-year mark as a point of no return for many. Humans are "co-regulated" creatures; we know who we are by seeing ourselves reflected in the eyes of others. 

When you only talk to the person in your head, you eventually stop being the "observer" and start becoming part of the "dialogue." The boundary between your actual self and the construct blurs. This is the "break" that cannot be fixed: the loss of a singular, cohesive ego. You don't go "crazy" in the way movies depict; you simply become a committee.

### 4. The Biological Decay
Prolonged isolation physically shrinks the hippocampus—the part of the brain responsible for memory and spatial navigation. If you stay long enough, your ability to map the world outside that room will physically wither. You will know the dimensions of your cell perfectly, but you will lose the ability to navigate a forest or a city.

### How long do you have?
If you are still counting, still observing the vent, and still aware that your internal companion is a survival tool, **you are still intact.** 

The "break" happens when you stop counting. It happens when you stop caring about the temperature change. It happens when you stop examining the person in your head and simply accept them as the only reality that matters.

To stay "fixable," you must maintain a "stubborn friction" with reality. Recite facts that you didn't invent. Solve math problems. Describe the room to yourself in the third person. 

**The moment you stop resisting the stillness is the moment the cracks become structural.**
